questions.q: List the supporting characters in "The Last Lesson" and give one defining trait for each, based on the text.
questions.a: Supporting characters include: M. Hamel (dedicated, patriotic, transformative), old Hauser (regretful, eager to learn), former mayor and postmaster (respectful, sorrowful), Wachter the blacksmith (informative, possibly sympathetic), the narrator's parents (pragmatic, neglectful of education). A wrong answer that only lists names without traits shows the student cannot move from identification to analysis. A trait like "M. Hamel is strict" without noting his change reveals a surface-level reading.

questions.q: Explain why the villagers sit at the back benches on the day of the last lesson. What does their presence signify?
questions.a: The villagers sit at the back to honor M. Hamel's forty years of service and to mourn the loss of their French language and identity. Their presence signifies collective guilt for having neglected education and a final act of resistance against cultural erasure. A wrong answer that says "they came to watch" misses the emotional and thematic weight. If a student thinks they are there to learn German, they have misunderstood the historical context and the villagers' motive.

questions.q: Read this short passage about a new character, the village priest, who enters the classroom during the last lesson: "The priest stood at the door, his hands folded, eyes moist. He did not speak, but blessed the children with a slow sign of the cross." Identify one trait of the priest and provide evidence from the passage.
questions.a: Trait: The priest is solemn and supportive of the French cause. Evidence: "eyes moist" shows grief; "blessed the children with a slow sign of the cross" shows a deliberate, sacred endorsement of their French identity. A wrong answer that calls him "religious" without linking to the context of the last lesson fails to apply character analysis to the specific situation. The student must connect the action to the story's conflict.

questions.q: Compare M. Hamel's attitude and behavior at the start of the story (as remembered by Franz) with his attitude during the last lesson. What does this change reveal about his character and the story's theme?
questions.a: Initially, M. Hamel is strict, uses a ruler, and is feared by Franz ("terrible iron ruler"). During the last lesson, he is "grave and gentle," wears fine clothes, teaches with infinite patience, and ends by writing "Vive La France." The change reveals his deep patriotism and love for his language; he transforms from a mere teacher into a symbol of French resistance. A wrong answer that only lists differences without interpreting the thematic significance (e.g., "he becomes nice") shows inability to analyze character as a vehicle for theme.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the blacksmith Wachter's comment "Don't go so fast, bub; you'll get to your school in plenty of time!" is mockery or kindness. Defend your judgment with textual evidence.
questions.a: It is kindness, not mockery. Evidence: Wachter has just read the bulletin-board announcing the German order; he knows it is the last French lesson. His tone is likely sympathetic, giving Franz permission to be late because the usual rules no longer matter. Franz misinterprets it as mockery due to his own guilt and dread. A wrong answer that insists on mockery ignores the context of the bulletin-board and Franz's unreliable perspective. The student must evaluate the gap between character perception and authorial intent.

questions.q: Write a diary entry from old Hauser's perspective on the evening of the last lesson, expressing his feelings about the day, M. Hamel, and the French language.
questions.a: A good entry will include: regret for not attending school earlier, description of holding the primer and crying, respect for M. Hamel's dedication, anger at the Prussian order, and a resolve to keep French alive. A poor entry will be generic ("I felt sad") without specific textual anchors (primer, spectacles, spelling with babies, "Vive La France"). The task tests the student's ability to inhabit a supporting character's voice using textual details.
